https://www.politico.eu/article/labour-c.text: LIVERPOOL, England — A parade of top politicians from the governing Labour Party headed through the doors of the POLITICO Pub during the party’s annual conference in Liverpool Monday — with plenty more to come . Labour is in a chipper mood after swapping out unpopular leader Keir Starmer for the telegenic, hopey-changey Andy Burnham. But there’s a hard road ahead: a high-stakes budget arrives in exactly a month, and Nigel Farage’s right-populist outfit Reform UK remains just two points behind Labour in the national opinion polls, according to our aggregator . Here are the snap takeaways from a flurry of frank conversations down the (traveling) POLITICO local. Advertisement Advertisement 1) Andy Burnham has some wind in his sails Britain’s new PM goes into his big conference speech Tuesday with at least one reason to feel cheerful: he seems to have dramatically shifted the British public’s view of politics itself. A majority of Brits say they believe his Labour Party has a real chance of winning the next election, whenever it comes. That’s the verdict of a new POLITICO Poll from Public First , unveiled at the pub Monday, and which captures the state of play after Burnham’s first two months as prime minister. It found 53% of voters believe Labour has a realistic shot at keeping power. That is a big increase from 33% in May — when Starmer was in the final stages of his doomed premiership. That was reflected in a bullish pub take from Lucy Powell, the Labour Party’s deputy leader. She told POLITICO she expects Labour to keep hold of the Holborn and St. Pancras seat at the upcoming parliamentary by-election triggered by Starmer’s exit from the political scene. Caveat alert: Powell felt pretty chirpy about the Gorton and Denton by-election – where the party under Starmer lost to the Greens — too. So bookmark this one. 2) But Labour still has its eyes on Farage Twelve months ago, all the main stage talk at Labour conference was about how Nigel Farage — then-ascendant in the polls — is a proper baddie. Advertisement Advertisement Keir Starmer (remember him?) focused his big speech on taking direct aim at Reform UK for refusing to “believe in Britain.” But it’s been a long year — Burnham is now closing that polling gap, and the Tories, booted from office in 2024, are showing nascent signs of a recovery. So is Labour switching back to its traditional foe? Not yet, party chair Bridget Phillipson told us. Reform, she said, remain “well-organized … are well-funded, and you know — they’re not going anywhere.” And she argued the Tories have a long, long road back to government. 3) Gordon Brown just can’t stop giving advice In the latest sign Labour can’t quite get over its 1990s heyday, two more Cabinet ministers revealed that former PM Gordon Brown is in regular contact with them. After Chancellor John Healey shed light on his own advice from Brown over the weekend, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told the POLITICO Pub he and Brown’s most recent interaction was a phone chat while Miliband was in New York at the U.N. General Assembly. “I had a late-night phone call with him actually last week,” Miliband said . “They come thick and fast.” Scotland Secretary Douglas Alexander told us he felt like consoling Healey about Brown’s stream of ALL-CAPS messages by telling him “the first 35 years is the worst and then you get over it.” Advertisement Advertisement 4) We’re starting to tease out how Labour’s big beasts really see the world Burnham’s ascent to the top of Labour saw a big changing of the guard in the U.K. cabinet. Previously domestic-focused ministers Ed Miliband and Wes Streeting – both from rival schools in the Labour movement — are now turning their attention to the world outside Westminster and getting pinned down on the specifics. In back-to-back POLITICO Pub interviews, Miliband — a Labour veteran who is now the U.K.’s foreign secretary — signalled a split with the Trump administration on the U.S. president’s bid to invite Russian President Vladimir Putin to the G20 in Miami. And he risked disappointing some of his supporters on Labour’s soft-left by batting away suggestions the U.K. should stump up reparations to Commonwealth nations for its role in the transatlantic slave trade. Streeting, for his turn, came over a little Mark Rutte. In a line that could have been uttered by the NATO chief, who has stressed the need to give Trump a hearing on European defense spending, Streeting warned Britain and Europe to get out of their “defensive crouch.” 5) Labour can’t quite shake the election question s Burnham may have gone into conference ruling out a snap election, but that hasn’t stopped the swirling speculation about how exactly the PM would cobble together a government if he falls short of a majority when voters do eventually go to the polls. Stephen Kinnock, the Welsh secretary, at least told the POLITICO Pub he cannot see Labour working with Plaid Cymru — which stormed to power in devolved elections earlier this year. Advertisement Advertisement Kinnock said: “If the condition for that coalition to work is that you would then agree to nationalism and separatism and the breakup of the United Kingdom, the answer is no.” 6) Shopping in London is about to get less awful London Mayor Sadiq Khan came armed with a newsline for his POLITICO Pub grilling. Khan, a three-time election-winning Labour stalwart who has often beefed with Donald Trump, revealed that a kilometer of London’s iconic Oxford Street will be pedestrianized next month . Just in time for the Christmas shopping chaos.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cwm2r2.text: Plummeting Israel flight like 'rollercoaster', says passenger Plummeting Israel flight like 'rollercoaster', says passenger Close A passenger on board Flight FZ1073, which fell 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes when a pilot apparently stabbed his co-pilot, told the BBC about his experience. The aircraft had been flying to Israel when the incident took place, which Almog Itali described as feeling like a "rollercoaster". The plane was diverted to Saudi Arabia after several passengers said they took control of the flight and two other pilots at the rear of the plane reportedly came forward to land the plane. https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/new.text: Kyiv: Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX on Wednesday of limiting Starlink services, crippling its drones, as Russian missiles knocked out power stations in attacks President Volodymyr Zelenskiy called ostentatious disrespect to Donald Trump.Kyiv's relationship with Washington has taken a sharp turn for the worse since US President Trump abruptly lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week and publicly turned on Zelenskiy.Trump, under political pressure to lower fuel prices that have soared since he launched a war against Iran, has called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries, and said Ukrainians should replace their wartime leader.Read more: Trump says 'massive' oil, gas and mineral exploration to begin in GreenlandThe US president also announced that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed to halt attacks on energy targets, although neither side confirmed this and the past two days have seen intensive Russian bombing, including of Ukrainian power stations.NO WARNING BEFORE STARLINK CUTSUkrainian military officials said Musk's SpaceX had without warning interrupted functioning of military-grade Starlink terminals moving at high speed, effectively preventing Kyiv from using them as onboard guides for drones. Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions, presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.Read more: Trump has learnt his India lesson the hard way. Will he own up?The apparent suggestion that Musk's company might limit Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf. Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you ​playing politics with your products again? Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski asked Musk on X. As your European customers, we are watching you. There was no immediate response from Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a small man . SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside of US business hours.Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the suggestion that SpaceX might limit Ukrainian capabilities reinforced wider Ukrainian concerns that Washington could withhold battlefield support to compel its one-time ally to make concessions.Sources have told Reuters and other news organisations that the US has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, to press Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries.NO WARNING AHEAD OF MISSILESRescue workers in Kyiv were stretchering the injured from the wreckage of a blasted-out residential building overnight, while firefighters battled a huge blaze in the darkness. Officials said 2 people were killed and 21 wounded at the site.Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russian missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Russia's defence ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelenskiy said more than 30 power stations were damaged.Ukrainian officials said late on Tuesday they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before the massive Russian attacks on the capital. Trump had insisted on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.Zelenskiy cast the latest attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump's declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets. Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong, Zelenskiy wrote on X. The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale - Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States. Zelenskiy has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russian refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Tuesday that contacts were continuing about an energy truce.Ukraine reported downing just 4 out of 39 Russian missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air-defences against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.Starlink does not work inside Russia, and Ukrainian drones hitting Russia's oil industry use other means of communication, but Ukraine uses Musk's system to guide drones over its own territory, including parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia. According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control, Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, said in a statement to Reuters.A source in Ukraine's defence ministry said the limitations significantly complicate logistics and some drone operations.Since being turned on over Ukraine in the early days of Russia's invasion in 2022, Starlink has been the lifeblood of Ukrainian battlefield communications.Its resistance to electronic signal jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones and drones used to drop supplies to frontline troops.
